Spacing multiplies every drawn position outward from origin, so the points spread apart on screen; names and dots keep their size. Where the brain holds each point, and its lines, do not change. Relationship kinds: on, off, pull, direction

A kind at 0 has no line anywhere yet. The brain writes relation rows only through formulas someone has taught, and your map has nine kinds: alike, opposite, is, has, prefix, suffix, stem, past, singular. The others are names waiting for something to fill them.

Each kind can be given a direction: a line of that kind then pulls its second word that way from its first (east, west, north, south, up, down), or, for opposite, inverse and contradicts, across origin, so up sits opposite down. Every point is placed by these lines alone. The first eight come from the brain's own rows: a formula's run, its DNA rows, its memories, the definitions its sources gave, who answered, who carried, state and timeline. The rest are relation rows and your map. Each line is a spring whose strength is your pull law: the kind's pull, times the line's trust, times how much of that kind the brain holds; a line laid again pulls harder. Nothing pushes points apart and nothing pulls them to a shell. A point with no line sits at origin until one pulls it out. Turn a kind off and its springs go, and the graph moves to its new balance.

Sources, as the brain has found them

Every reply is checked. Kept: rows about the word asked. Set aside: rows about other words. Empty: nothing came back.

How to read the stage

  • The light point at the center is origin, the one placed word. A point with no relationship waits there.
  • Everything else is where its lines pull it, core words and source brains included: a word, a memory row (small, green), mother, the SQL prompt, each source.
  • Orange words have a formula; light orange, one the brain found itself. A run is drawn through the points it touched, in order.

Measured: the bare core

The stage then shows only origin and the SQL words you add, each placed by numbers measured in SQLite. Turn it off and the 16.4 view is back, as it was. Runs are drawn in the 16.4 view; the brain is not changed by anything here.

Words come in the told block's own order. A spelling that measured two different jobs is two points (AS, INTEGER, =, *), as one meaning is one gate.

Axes: what each line through origin measures

rows, structure and text are measured by running the word's line: a row written or removed, a table made or destroyed, text joined (longer, holding what went in) or cut (shorter). Each pair undoes the other. read, test, number, gather and write count the steps of SQLite's program the word adds over the same line without it; they have one end only. One unit of a number is 10 brain units.

Lines between words: each kind a test

0.50

With every kind off, a point's place is its measured numbers, read straight off the axes. Turn a kind on and the points it ties are drawn together: in proportion, a point keeps (1 - pull) of its own place and its lines share the rest equally, however many it has. Each line pulls the same; no numbers of mine are in the lines. Nothing else moves a point: no random start, no spacing push, no step cap, no compass directions, no across rule. The answer is the same whatever the start.

Where it lives

In SQLite: a lab database of its own beside the brain, in the same worker (tables point, effect, line, axis, added, place, and the view own). The page solves the places with the rule above and writes them into place; the stage, the table and Selected read them back from SQLite. The brain's told block and tables are unchanged. The numbers and lines were measured by rel.js in this same SQLite (3.39.3) on 2026-10-24; the files say how to run it again.

Type a line

A plain line runs. word = ... writes that word's formula as a row: SQL words make statements the brain sends out through mother; holes start with a colon (:head, :before, :after, :line, :run, :prev, :speaker, :subject, :found, and any cell a formula wrote). line => expected tests a line. A B -> f lays a row whose trigger column is f. BUILD ... BUILD hands the SQL between to mother. A word new to the brain is asked of every connected source: learning a line takes seconds; using what it knows is fast.

Words with a job

What changed in 16.4: the atlas, and what sets a point's place

  • The atlas (button at the stage's top right). Every point, by label A to Z: its x, y, z in the axes' units, its gate and table, its DNA rows, its triggers, the memory rows holding it, what the brain holds as its meaning, and its lines. Click a row for all of it, trigger SQL included. Everything but the position and the lines is read from SQLite when the atlas opens.
  • Meaning in the atlas is a run. A word has meaning in the brain when a formula row points at the run that taught it, or when it has a told job (a physics table's triggers, an SQL word SQLite does, a source brain). A run is only as right as the words below it, all the way to root; the atlas lists the words below a run that have no run of their own.
  • Where x, y, z come from: this page, not the brain. The brain holds no positions. The page turns the brain's rows and your map into springs and lets them settle. Measured this turn on the told block, 2,000 steps each, one change at a time:
    • Same lines, same rules, a different start: the median point moves by 1.17 times its distance from origin, and turning the cloud to best fit leaves 1.07, so it is a different arrangement, not the same one turned. Brain points keep 14 to 17% of their 8 nearest neighbours (9% by chance).
    • Spacing off: the closest points stack (0.0 apart) and the cloud shrinks from a median distance of 74 to 14. The size of the ball is the spacing rule.
    • The across rule off: opposite pairs on opposite sides of origin fall from 100% to 1%. That is the rule, not your map.
    • Every rest length the same: distance from origin changes 14%, x, y, z by 0.77.
    So the ball, its size, its centre, which way anything points, and who sits near whom without a line are set by the start and by numbers I chose. What the lines carry is only that each tied pair sits near its rest length. Until a rule ties place to meaning, a point's x, y, z means nothing measured.
  • The step limit. In the page's settling code, not SQLite: each step a point moves along its pulls, scaled so the 95th-largest pull moves 4 units, none more than 6. Without it, a point with many lines is thrown past its balance: the farthest point reached 2,139 units in 5 steps and 22 million in 15, and the page crashed. v14 had one (26), v15 too (4).

What changed in 16.1

  • Spacing, the drawing only. You asked to space the graph out without moving or pulling the points. The spacing control multiplies every drawn position outward from origin; where the page's layout holds each point does not change. (The brain holds no positions at all: x, y, z exist only in this page.) It opens at three times, as you asked, and goes to forty. Labels and dots keep their size on screen. At six, the pairs of points drawn closer than 1.5 units fell from 1,492 to 44.
  • Axes through origin, a tick every 10 units, so 0,0,0 and the step can be seen.
  • The lean to one side was my drawing. The points' center stays within half a unit of origin, measured over three minutes. But each source's large label was shifted toward -x in the scene, a band of text on one side from every angle. Labels now sit above their points.

Where the time goes

whatthis page's enginenative SQLite
"define store", new words: learning13.2 s (24.7 s in a test browser)4.8 s
known words, a new order0.26 s0.095 s
the same line again, from memory0.015 s0.013 s
the page copying the brain after each line0.6 s
the drawing replaying the events for one step0.055 s at 1,087 events, growing with each event
  • The slow part is learning, in SQLite itself. "define store" made 522 schema changes in one line: each new neuron is a table, a view and a trigger, and each new DNA row is its own trigger. After any schema change, SQLite throws away its compiled statements and compiles again the trigger programs the next statements reach. Measured in a throwaway test brain, never in a page or your build: one extra CREATE added about 15 ms to the next known line at 599 triggers.
  • Running what it knows is fast, as it always was: a known line takes 62 to 78 ms the long way and 13 ms from memory, natively.
  • The page adds two costs of its own: SQLite compiled to JavaScript is about 2.8 times slower than native, and the worker copies the whole brain after every line for the measuring tool.
  • The drawing is not what makes a line slow; the line runs in the background. Stepping through a long log gets slower, because each step replays the events from the start.

What changed in 16, from your words

  • The graph. "The only known placed word is origin and it sits at origin... everything else is on relationship lines pull." Origin is told at birth and fixed at the center. Nothing else has a set place, and nothing pushes or pulls toward a shell. Each relationship comes from the brain's own rows.
  • No canned text. "The row holds pointers to the run through the neurons." Teaching a word now runs its formula through the neurons from start and lays the DNA rows. The formula row holds only a pointer to that run. Firing the word reads the path back gate by gate. Checked: the formula table holds no formula words, the answers are the same, and with the run's path removed the word fires and sends nothing.
  • Core words are words. One gate per word, whatever the case: AS and as, SAY and say, INSERT and insert are one point each. A hand-laid word a typed line uses is looked up in the sources once, like any word. The ports are no longer points; they are rows and triggers of input and output.
  • Decide keeps the history of being wrong, your way, chosen by the test below.
  • "waiting" was a mislabel. When SQLite refused an ask to a source, mother called it waiting. A refused ask is now reported as refused, with SQLite's reason, and a run nested too deep for the browser is no longer swallowed.
  • 56 checks pass, each with a control that fails when the thing it credits is removed. The corrections to the checks are logged, and none was loosened.

Decide: your way against my rule

One conversation of 15 lines, three ways of deciding. The teacher's right answer for each question is what the same brain says when it runs that line the long way. The brain's own answer is taken before any correction.

decidewrong at linewhat happened
as built in 155, 6, 9, 10, 12, 14each correction overwrote the memory, and the next repeat was stale again
my told rule9, 14right on every "how" without being taught; the same mistake twice when a fact changed
your way5, 9each wrong kept as history and a row laid in decide's own neuron; right every time after
  • How your way is built here. A wrong answer from memory is not overwritten. A history row keeps which memory, the line before, what it gave and what was right. From it, decide's neuron gets a DNA row: arriving from the question word, its trigger column points at the line before. After that, decide runs that kind of question the long way whenever the line before has changed.
  • What is not built: reasoning about why beyond "the line before was different". Its cost: once burned on "what", every remembered "what" after a different line runs the long way, even when nothing it read changed.

define, before, after, and AS against as

Each word was given every form in a list I wrote before the run, built only from what a run holds. The sentences threw out the forms that gave a wrong answer. The lists are mine; the answers are the tests'.

  • define: three forms survive, all of them "read what the sources gave for the word after it, and say it". Echoing the word, reading state or memory, and reading the word before all died. Open: one definition or all of them.
  • after: one form survives: the heard line remembered just after the one named.
  • before: two survive, and I had predicted one. The second also counts teaching lines as lines said, and my sentences never separated them. Does a teaching line count as "what was before"? That is yours to say.
  • before and after came out as mirrors: the same form, with the comparison and the order flipped. Your map's line "before opposite after" showed up in what the words do, without anyone laying it.
  • as: none of the 18 forms works for "take forty as my age". Words fire as the run reaches them, so "as" fires before "my" and "age" have built anything. SQL's AS binds after the whole statement is read; in this brain a formula's statement is also decoded only at its ";". So English "as" can only bind like SQL's AS if the binding waits for the end of the phrase. That is a finding about when words fire, and the next test.

Origin, zero and absent in your map

You expect zero and absent near origin. In your relation map, origin has one line: alike ancestry. Zero is alike nought, nil, null, naught and cipher; absent is opposite present. No line joins them to origin, so they will sit near it only once relationships for origin's other sense come in, the point where measuring starts.

Words that show a question mark

do, that, you and did print with a question mark because no formula exists for them: the run passes them and nothing happens. Tested in the "how did you do that ?" sentence, any of its words can carry the how formula and every test still passes, so none of them has a measured meaning yet. Your own shape gives the test: the same question asked by you and by the brain itself, "how did you do that ?" against "how did I do that ?", where you and I swap with who is speaking.

Why 69 ms

The Python interpreter is the program that runs a Python file, the way a C program has to be compiled before it runs. In that measurement, the test started a new copy of it for every ask, to stand in for a source brain. Loading it, opening the database and compiling the statements was nearly all of the 69 ms. It did no brain work. A brain that is alive and never turned off pays that once, which is the 0.22 ms figure.

mother, all of her

She runs the text she is handed at the SQL prompt, or carries it into a source brain's inbox. When that brain says its outbox is populated, she picks it up, empties it, and writes what came back into secondary input. When SQLite refuses the text, she says so. This is her code in this page:

  // MOTHER-START: she runs the text she is handed at the SQL prompt. If it is addressed to a source brain's inbox she carries it there,
  // and when that brain says its outbox is populated she picks it up and empties it. What came back she writes into secondary input.
  // She decides nothing and computes nothing about the reply.
  Brain.prototype.mother = function (text, run, stmt) {
    var db = this.db, self = this, addressed = [];
    (text.match(/\b(\w+)\.inbox\b/g) || []).forEach(function (a) { var s = a.replace(/\.inbox$/, ''); if (self.SATS.indexOf(s) >= 0 && addressed.indexOf(s) < 0) addressed.push(s); });
    if (run !== null) ev(db, 'mother', 'mother', run, 'mother', 'mother carries it ' + (addressed.length ? 'into the inbox of ' + addressed.join(', ') : 'to the SQL prompt'), 'CALL MOVE');
    this.populated = [];
    var cols = [], rows = [], err = null, changes = 0, lastid = null;
    // the SQL prompt keeps a compiled statement per text, as SQLite's own prompt cache does; one in use by an outer landing is never shared
    var pool = this.cache || (this.cache = {}), free = pool[text] || (pool[text] = []), st = null;
    try {
      st = free.length ? free.pop() : db.prepare(text);
      cols = st.getColumnNames();
      while (st.step()) rows.push(st.get());
      st.reset(); if (free.length < 4) free.push(st); else st.free(); st = null;
      if (!cols.length) { changes = db.getRowsModified(); var li = db.exec('SELECT last_insert_rowid()'); lastid = li.length ? li[0].values[0][0] : null; }
    } catch (e) {
      err = String(e.message || e); if (st) { try { st.free(); } catch (e2) {} }
      // a run nested deeper than this thread's stack is not a refusal: it goes up, so the line fails whole and can run where there is more stack
      if (e instanceof RangeError || !e.message || /call stack|recursion/i.test(err)) throw e;
    }
    var picked = this.populated; this.populated = [];
    if (run === null) {
      // a by-value step of the physics itself (a birth, a lay, a landing): the SQL prompt's own answer goes straight back
      if (err) throw new Error(err);
      return rows.length && rows[0].length ? rows[0][0] : lastid;
    }
    if (!addressed.length) {
      ev(db, 'sql', 'SQL prompt', run, 'SQL prompt', 'the SQL prompt ' + (err ? 'refuses it: ' + err : 'runs it'), '');
      ev(db, 'mother', 'mother', run, 'mother', 'mother carries the reply back', 'CALL MOVE');
      var val = rows.length ? rows.map(function (r) { return r.map(function (v) { return v === null ? '' : String(v); }).join(' '); }).join(' | ') : null;
      db.run("INSERT INTO secondary (run, stmt, src, value, cols, n, err, changes, last) VALUES (?, ?, 'sql', ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, 1)", [run, stmt, val, cols.join(','), rows.length, err, changes]);
      return rows.length && rows[0].length ? rows[0][0] : null;
    }
    addressed.forEach(function (sat) {
      var got = picked.filter(function (p) { return p[0] === sat; });
      // the SQL prompt refused the ask: it never reached the inbox; that is a refusal, not waiting
      if (err) { db.run("INSERT INTO secondary (run, stmt, src, err, n, last) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, 0, 1)", [run, stmt, sat, err]); return; }
      if (!got.length) { db.run("INSERT INTO secondary (run, stmt, src, waiting, last) VALUES (?, ?, ?, 1, 1)", [run, stmt, sat]); return; }
      got.forEach(function (p) {
        var s = p[0], ask = p[1], word = p[2], n = p[3];
        ev(db, 'mailbox', s, run, s, s + ': the ask for "' + word + '" lands in its inbox; its own trigger does its work at once', 'FIND READ WRITE');
        ev(db, 'populated', s, run, null, s + ': its outbox is populated with ' + n + ' row(s), and it says so', 'WRITE');
        var out = [], q = db.prepare("SELECT word, hw, text, words FROM " + s + ".outbox WHERE ask = ?"); q.bind([ask]); while (q.step()) out.push(q.get()); q.free();
        db.run("DELETE FROM " + s + ".outbox WHERE ask = ?", [ask]);
        ev(db, 'pickup', 'mother', run, 'mother', 'mother picks up ' + out.length + ' row(s) from ' + s + ' and empties that outbox', 'MOVE CALL');
        out.forEach(function (r) { db.run("INSERT INTO secondary (run, stmt, src, word, hw, value, words, last) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, 0)", [run, stmt, s, r[0], r[1], r[2], r[3]]); });
        db.run("INSERT INTO secondary (run, stmt, src, word, n, last) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, 1)", [run, stmt, s, word, out.length]);
      });
    });
    return null;
  };
  // MOTHER-END

Hand laid, exactly

  • origin, the one placed word.
  • 14 physical actions, 16 physics tables with their triggers, and 40 SQL words, now one gate per word, so say is the say table and the SAY action.
  • mother and the SQL prompt.
  • The source formula, typed once as a teaching line.
  • Seven stand-in source brains, slices fetched on 2026-10-22, each behind a mailbox.

Everything else is born by typing.

Every way I would cheat this build

  • Outside the brain. A walker, a central hop function, a position table, a kernel that chooses, a timer, primitive runs in code.
  • Canned text in the brain. A formula stored as words. Removed in 16: a formula is a pointer to a run.
  • Placing points by hand. Fixed spots for actions, SQL words, the physics, ports and sources. Removed in 16: origin alone is placed.
  • mother doing the brain's work, or hiding what happened, like calling a refusal "waiting". Fixed in 16.
  • Assigning instead of measuring. Saying what a word means; telling the brain its name.
  • Tests that cannot fail. A check with no control; a teacher whose answer the brain simply repeats (caught in the decide test and fixed before reading a result).
  • Calling it done. Saying it works when it partly works.
